text:
Flee? But where? We cannot get out! And we cannot go to Kristin!

JEAN

Well then! Into my room? Necessity knows no law; and you can trust me,
for I am your true, sincere, and respectful friend!

MISS JULIE

But think!—suppose they look for you there?

JEAN

I shall bolt the door, and if anyone tries to break in, I shall shoot!—Come!

On his knees.

Come!

MISS JULIE

meaningfully.

Do you promise me—

JEAN

I swear!

Miss Julie exits hastily to the right. Jean rushes after her.

BALLET

The country folk enter in festive dress, with flowers in their hats; a
fiddler at their head; a keg of small beer and a small cask of brandy,
decorated with greenery, are set on the table; glasses are brought out.
Then they drink. Afterward they form a ring and sing and dance the singing
game: “There Came Two Ladies from the Woods.”

When this is over, they leave, still singing.

Miss Julie enters alone; sees the devastation in the kitchen; clasps her
hands; then picks up a powder puff and powders her face.

JEAN

enters; exalted.

There, you see! And you have heard! Do you consider it possible to remain
here?

MISS JULIE

No! I do not! But what, then, are we to do?

JEAN

Flee, travel, far away from here!

MISS JULIE

Travel? Yes, but where?

JEAN

To Switzerland, to the Italian lakes;—you have never been there?

MISS JULIE

No! Is it beautiful there?

JEAN

Oh, an eternal summer, orange trees, laurels, oh!

MISS JULIE

But what shall we do there afterward?

JEAN

There I shall establish a hotel with first-class goods and first-class
customers.

MISS JULIE

A hotel?

JEAN

That is a life, believe me; constantly new faces, new languages; not a
minute’s leisure for brooding or nerves; no searching for something to do,
for the work presents itself; night and day, the bell ringing, the train
whistling, the omnibus coming and going; while the gold pieces roll onto
the bureau. That is a life!

MISS JULIE

Yes, that is living! And I?

JEAN

Mistress of the house; the ornament of the firm. With your looks and your
manner—oh—it is a certain success! Colossal! You sit like a queen in the
office and set the slaves in motion by pressing an electric button; the
guests file past your throne and timidly lay their tribute on your table—you
would never believe how people tremble when they are handed a bill—I shall
salt the accounts, and you shall sugar them with your loveliest smile—ah!
let us travel away from here—

Takes a timetable from his pocket.

at once, on the next train!—we shall be in Malmö at six thirty; Hamburg at
eight forty early tomorrow morning; Frankfurt—Basel in one day, and in Como
by the Gotthard Railway in, let me see, three days! Three days!

MISS JULIE

All that is well and good! But Jean—you must give me courage—say that you
love me! Come and embrace me!

JEAN

hesitating.

I want to—but I dare not! Not here in this house anymore! I love you—without
a doubt—can you doubt it?

MISS JULIE

shyly, truly womanly.

Not “you”!—Say “thou”! There are no barriers between us anymore!—Say “thou”!

JEAN

in anguish.

I cannot!—There are still barriers between us, as long as we remain in this
house—there is the past, there is the Count—and I have never met anyone for
whom I have such respect—I need only see his gloves lying on a chair, and I
feel small—I need only hear the bell upstairs, and I start like a skittish
horse—and when I now see his boots standing there so straight and
self-assured, I feel my back bending!

Kicks the boots.

Superstition, prejudices that we have been taught since childhood—but that
one can forget just as easily. Just come to another country where there is
a republic, and people fall flat on their faces before my doorman’s livery—on
their faces they shall fall, you see; but I shall not! I was not born to
fall on my face, for there is substance in me, there is character, and once
I get hold of the first branch, you shall see me climb!

I am a servant today, but next year I shall be a proprietor, in ten years I
shall be a man of independent means, and then I shall travel to Romania,
have myself decorated, and may—mark well, I say may—end as a count!

MISS JULIE

Beautiful, beautiful!

JEAN

Ah, in Romania one buys oneself the title of count, and then you will be a
countess after all! My countess!

MISS JULIE

What do I care about all that, which I am now casting behind me!—Say that
you love me, otherwise—yes, what am I otherwise?

JEAN

I shall say it a thousand times—afterward—only not here! And above all, no
feelings, unless everything is to be lost! We must approach the matter
coldly! Like sensible people!

Takes out a cigar, clips and lights it.

Now sit down there! Then I shall sit here, and we shall talk as though
nothing had happened!

MISS JULIE

despairingly.

Oh my God! Have you no feelings, then?

JEAN

I! There is no one as full of feeling as I am; but I can restrain myself.

MISS JULIE

Just now you could kiss my shoe—and now!

JEAN

harshly.

Yes, that was then! Now we have other things to think about!

MISS JULIE

Do not speak harshly to me!

JEAN

No, but sensibly! One folly has been committed; do not commit more! The
Count may be here at any moment, and before then our fates must be decided.
What do you think of my plans for the future? Do you approve of them?

MISS JULIE

They seem quite acceptable to me, but just one question: so large an
enterprise requires considerable capital; do you have it?

JEAN

chews the cigar.

I! Certainly! I have my professional knowledge, my vast experience, my
knowledge of languages! That is capital of real worth, I should think!

MISS JULIE

But with that you cannot even buy a railway ticket.

JEAN

That is certainly true; but that is why I am looking for a backer who can
advance the funds!

MISS JULIE

Where will you find one in such haste?

JEAN

You shall find one, if you are willing to become my partner!

MISS JULIE

I cannot, and I own nothing myself.

Pause.

JEAN

Then the whole matter falls through—

MISS JULIE

And—

JEAN

Things will remain as they are!

MISS JULIE

Do you think I shall remain under this roof as your mistress? Do you think
I am willing to let the people point their fingers at me; do you imagine I
can look my father in the face after this? No! Take me away from here: from
the humiliation and the disgrace!—Oh, what have I done, my God, my God!
